result.reason: The passage presents the tannaitic dispute (ke-tanai) where the first tanna holds that usage alone by the second party exempts the first, which is precisely what the 'Tannaim Debate' prose describes.

Both items together present the gemara's clarification of what the dispute is about (b'mai kamipalgi) and explain both sides of the breira concept, which matches 'Breira Defined' prose perfectly — that section explicitly describes the gemara asking b'mai kamipalgi and explaining the concept of breira in jointly held property.

Both items discuss the partners-who-vowed-not-to-benefit dispute about entering a jointly held courtyard/field and its underlying yesh/ein breira logic, which is precisely what the 'Field Prohibition' prose describes.

Both items present Rabbi Elazar's ruling about selling a cistern and the gemara's question/answer about how handing over the bucket effects acquisition — exactly what the 'Selling Well' prose describes, including the initial puzzle and the resolution that it serves as authorization for chazakah, before the parallel 'House Keys' case.

The passage presents Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi's ruling about selling a house via key transfer, followed by the exact gemara challenge and 'le'olam b'chazakah' resolution, which matches perfectly the 'House Keys' section's prose description of that same ruling and its reinterpretation.

Both items together present exactly the ruling about selling a flock via the mashkukhit and the gemara's objection/resolution that handing it over equals 'lech meshoch u-knei' — precisely what candidate 0's prose describes.

The passage covers both the identification of the mashkukhit (bell vs. lead goat) and the Galilean's teaching about blinding the lead goat, which together form the content described in the 'Mashchuchis ID' prose, not the 'Locks & Punishment' section which treats the Galilean teaching as merely a side note to other material.

All four items are the Mishnah's halakhot about pit liability (covering, appropriate covering, falling forward/backward, ox with implements, deaf ox, children/slaves), and the 'Mishnah Setup' prose explicitly discusses every one of these sub-cases in the same order.

The passage covers both the exemption for proper covering and the gemara's question of how anything fell in, which is exactly what the 'Proper Cover' prose discusses — the answer from Rabbi Yitzchak bar bar Ḥana is the punchline to that question and belongs with it, not as a separate section.

The passage poses the camel-weakening dilemma and gives the gemara's initial two-case resolution (common vs. uncommon camels), which matches exactly the prose of 'Camel Weakening' where the question is introduced and the gemara asks 'what are the circumstances?'

The passage introduces the 'occasionally' (l'prakim) case as the necessary focus, which directly matches candidate 0's prose that sets up the three-tiered framework and identifies the occasional camel as the case the gemara is actually pursuing, before candidate 1's prose then elaborates the unresolved question in detail.

Both items together form the gemara's attempt to derive from the mishnah that occasional camels render the owner an ones (not a poshea), which is precisely what section 2 'Proof from First Part' describes: the gemara reads the mishnah as a case of d'atu l'prakim camels weakening the cover, concluding the owner is exempt and apparently an ones.
All 12 items form the sustained gemara analysis attempting to resolve the migo question through multiple readings of both mishna clauses, which is exactly what candidate 4's prose describes.

The passage contains the full baraita and migo argument in one unit — the gemara introduces the proof about vulnerable animals, draws the exemption for the standard ox, raises the migo challenge, and rejects it — and candidate 0's prose explicitly describes 'what the gemara presents as a stronger proof' returning to the mishnah clause about deaf/blind/nighttime oxen, which is the opening of this entire passage.
